title: Aortic stenosis: recognising and grading it

source.citation: Patel H, Lewis BW, Paulus R. Aortic Stenosis: Diagnosis and Treatment. Am Fam Physician. 2026;114(2):148-155.

questions.q: Which examination finding most raises the likelihood of aortic stenosis?
d: A holosystolic murmur at the apex
questions.why: Its positive likelihood ratio is 15.7. The next strongest signs are a murmur radiating to both carotids (12) and a delayed carotid upstroke (6.3).

questions.q: Which of these are classic symptoms of aortic stenosis?
questions.why: Aortic stenosis stays silent through a long latent period, and these symptoms usually appear only once the valve is severely narrowed.

questions.q: A 74-year-old has a new systolic murmur and fatigue. What is the preferred first test?
questions.why: Echo is noninvasive, relatively cheap, and grades severity in the same study. Calcium scoring and stress testing come in only when symptoms remain unexplained after echo.

questions.q: Which set of echo findings defines severe aortic stenosis?
questions.a: Valve area under 1 cm², Vmax over 4 m/s, mean gradient 40 mm Hg or more
d: Valve area 1.0 to 1.5 cm², Vmax 3.0 to 3.9 m/s, gradient 20 to 39 mm Hg
Valve area over 1.5 cm², Vmax 2.0 to 2.9 m/s, gradient under 20 mm Hg
Valve area under 1.5 cm², Vmax over 3 m/s, gradient over 30 mm Hg
questions.why: Patients are often asymptomatic until Vmax passes 4 m/s, which is why severe stenosis can be a surprise on a routine echo.

questions.q: An echo shows valve area 0.8 cm², Vmax 3.4 m/s and mean gradient 28 mm Hg. How is this classified?
questions.why: A reduced stroke volume underestimates both velocity and gradient, but the small valve area and the physiology are those of severe disease, so it is managed as severe.

questions.q: How reliable is auscultation alone for detecting significant valvular disease?
questions.why: The absence of a murmur is more useful than its presence: it has a negative predictive value of 88% for significant valvular disease.

questions.q: Which risk factors for aortic stenosis are nonmodifiable?
questions.why: More than half of people with a bicuspid valve eventually need it replaced, often a decade or more earlier than those with three leaflets.

questions.q: A patient with aortic stenosis has gastrointestinal bleeding with no obvious source. Which syndrome should be considered?
questions.why: Heyde syndrome is acquired von Willebrand disease caused by the stenotic valve; replacing the valve improves the bleeding tendency.

questions.q: About what share of patients with aortic stenosis also have atrial fibrillation, and how does that affect valve replacement?
questions.a: About 16%, and they are less likely to get valve replacement
d: About 16%, and they are more likely to get valve replacement
About 50%, and they are less likely to get valve replacement
About 2%, and there is no difference
questions.why: The problem is attribution: dyspnea and fatigue get blamed on the arrhythmia, so the stenosis goes unreferred. The hazard ratio for replacement at one year was 0.73.

questions.q: What is the characteristic murmur of aortic stenosis?
questions.a: Loud, late-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, radiating to the carotids
d: Blowing holosystolic murmur at the apex, radiating to the axilla
Early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border
Continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle
questions.why: The peak of the murmur moves later as stenosis worsens, which is why a later-peaking murmur is a trigger for repeat echo.

questions.q: How does aortic sclerosis differ from stenosis, and how often does it progress?
questions.a: Calcification without restricted leaflet movement; about 2% progress to stenosis each year
d: Calcification with restricted leaflets; about 20% progress each year
Leaflet thickening without calcification; it almost never progresses
A congenital two-leaflet valve; half eventually need replacement
questions.why: Sclerosis puts a patient in stage A, where the only management is modifying cardiovascular risk factors.

questions.q: Asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis, ejection fraction 60%, Vmax 4.3 m/s, no other surgery planned. What stage is this, and what does it call for?
questions.a: Stage C: refer to cardiology; repeat echo in 6 to 12 months if replacement is not indicated
d: Stage B: repeat echo in 1 to 2 years
questions.why: Stage C becomes an indication for replacement if the ejection fraction drops under 50%, Vmax passes 5 m/s, a stress test is positive, or Vmax rises more than 0.3 m/s in a year.

questions.q: What is the estimated two-year mortality of untreated symptomatic severe aortic stenosis?
questions.why: Valve replacement is the only treatment that changes that number, which is why symptoms in severe stenosis mean prompt referral rather than watchful waiting.

questions.q: Which early or atypical symptoms of aortic stenosis are commonly attributed to aging instead?
questions.why: Older patients blame these on age, and so do clinicians, which is why the guideline puts a careful history at the centre of diagnosis.
